hypotheses.title: initiateClose callable by anyone, enabling griefing of active channels
hypotheses.description: initiateClose() has no access control. Any external actor can start the grace period on any open channel, even one the payer intends to keep active. Once gracePeriodEnd is set, the channel cannot be re-opened or extended, and after GRACE_PERIOD anyone can call finalize() to force-close it, refunding the payer and terminating the streaming relationship.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker calls initiateClose(victimChannelId) on a channel they do not own. 2) gracePeriodEnd is set to now + 1 hour. 3) After 1 hour, attacker (or anyone) calls finalize(channelId), forcing closure. 4) Payee loses the ability to settle further vouchers; payer's channel is terminated prematurely.
hypotheses.impact: Denial of service on active payment channels; payee cannot continue receiving streaming payments; payer's channel is force-closed against their intent.
hypotheses.recommendation: Restrict initiateClose() to channel.payer (and/or channel.payee), or require an authorization signature.

hypotheses.title: close() lacks expiry check allowing stale voucher settlement
hypotheses.description: The `close()` function verifies the voucher signature but never checks `block.timestamp > voucher.expiry`, unlike `settle()`. A voucher that has already expired (and thus should no longer be redeemable) can still be settled via the cooperative close path. This lets a payee force settlement of an expired voucher as long as they can obtain the payer's CLOSE signature.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Payer signs a voucher with a short expiry and later signs a CLOSE authorization for a cooperative close. 2) The close transaction is delayed past `voucher.expiry`. 3) Payee (or anyone holding both signatures) calls `close()` after expiry; the missing expiry check lets the stale voucher settle and drains the channel.
hypotheses.impact: Expired vouchers remain redeemable, defeating the expiry safety mechanism and allowing funds to be settled against the payer's intent.
hypotheses.recommendation: Add `if (block.timestamp > voucher.expiry) revert VoucherExpired();` at the start of `close()`.

hypotheses.title: initiateClose permissionless allows griefing payee out of settlement window
hypotheses.description: `initiateClose()` has no access control — any external address (including the payer, a griefer, or the payee) can call it for any channel. Once called, `gracePeriodEnd` is set and any subsequent settlement will still work (settle doesn't check gracePeriodEnd), so it's not a true block. But `finalize()` requires `gracePeriodEnd != 0`, and after grace expires anyone (including payer) can finalize, refunding remaining deposit and marking finalized — cutting off future settlement for any in-flight vouchers. An attacker (e.g., the payer to avoid paying) can call `initiateClose` immediately after opening a channel, wait `GRACE_PERIOD`, then call `finalize()`, permanently preventing the payee from settling any vouchers signed after the finalize (settle reverts with ChannelAlreadyFinalized).
hypotheses.attackPath: Attacker (payer, or any address on behalf) calls `initiateClose(channelId)` right after opening channel. Waits `GRACE_PERIOD`. Calls `finalize(channelId)`, receiving full deposit refund. Any vouchers the payee holds (e.g., for services rendered during the window) become unenforceable because `settle()` reverts with `ChannelAlreadyFinalized()`.
hypotheses.impact: Payer can consume metered services (get signed vouchers) and then grief the payee by finalizing before payee submits them; payee loses earned stablecoin payments while payer gets a full refund. Direct loss of funds for the payee.
hypotheses.recommendation: Restrict `initiateClose()` to the payer (or payee), and/or require the payee to consent, or extend finalize to require payee-submitted final voucher; at minimum, ensure `finalize()` cannot run before any voucher signed/known is settled.

hypotheses.title: finalize() callable by anyone locks out payee without honoring unsettled vouchers
hypotheses.description: `finalize()` has no access control — any address can call it after the grace period. It refunds the payer and marks the channel finalized. If the payee holds an un-settled voucher (or the grace period elapses before payee's settlement tx lands), `settle()` reverts because `channel.finalized == true`, so the payee's earned amount is unrecoverable on-chain. The payee has no recourse. The settlement window is entirely at the mercy of when `initiateClose` was called and whether the payee can act within `GRACE_PERIOD`.
hypotheses.attackPath: Payer initiates close, immediately after observes a new voucher was issued but not yet settled. Pays no further attention. A griefer (or the payer) calls `finalize()` exactly when grace expires, refunding the deposit to payer. Payee's voucher for services provided is permanently unenforceable (`settle()` reverts).
hypotheses.impact: Payee's earned stablecoins are lost; payer receives undeserved refund. Broken economic settlement model for the entire MPP use case.
hypotheses.recommendation: Require payee consent (signature) in `finalize()`, or allow payee to submit final voucher at finalize time; alternatively restrict `finalize()` to payee.

hypotheses.title: addDeposit accepts deposits from anyone, does not credit depositor
hypotheses.description: `addDeposit()` transfers `amount` from `msg.sender` but credits `channel.deposit -= ` to the channel, and refunds during finalize/close go entirely to `channel.payer`. There is no restriction that `msg.sender == channel.payer`. Any third party (including a griefer) can add deposit to a channel, effectively donating tokens to the payer (who will receive the refund at finalize/close). More importantly, a griefer can grief by force-funding, or an unsuspecting user's tokens go to the wrong recipient.
hypotheses.attackPath: Attacker calls `addDeposit(channelId, amount)` on a channel where they are not payer. Their tokens are transferred but the eventual refund goes to the original `channel.payer`. Alternatively, an attacker calls with tiny amounts to alter `channel.deposit` before finalize in a way that affects refund accounting—not exploitable for gain but causes loss to depositor.
hypotheses.impact: Depositor loses tokens sent to a channel they don't own (refund goes to payer). Funds are misdirected; griefing is possible.
hypotheses.recommendation: Require `msg.sender == channel.payer` in `addDeposit()`, or track per-depositor contribution with refund to depositor.

hypotheses.title: openChannel deadline parameter is never enforced
hypotheses.description: `openChannel()` accepts a `deadline` parameter but never checks `block.timestamp <= deadline`. The parameter is unused, so a transaction signed with a deadline can be included arbitrarily late. This is a meta-transaction-style issue: if the payer signed an off-chain authorization with a deadline, the on-chain call ignores it, allowing stale authorizations to be executed.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Payer signs an off-chain authorization to open a channel with a specific deadline. 2) A relayer holds the transaction past the deadline. 3) The relayer submits `openChannel()` after the deadline; the contract accepts it because the deadline is not checked, locking the payer's deposit into a channel they no longer want.
hypotheses.impact: Stale authorizations can be executed, locking payer funds into unwanted channels.
hypotheses.recommendation: Add `if (block.timestamp > deadline) revert DeadlineExpired();` at the start of `openChannel()`.

hypotheses.title: addDeposit allows anyone to fund any channel and grief payer
hypotheses.description: addDeposit() has no check that msg.sender is the channel's payer. Any external actor can call it for any open channel, pulling tokens from their own balance into the channel's deposit. While the attacker loses their own funds, this inflates channel.deposit and can be used to grief accounting, distort getAvailableBalance, and complicate finalize/close refund math (payerRefund = deposit - settled grows, but the extra funds are stuck and refunded to the payer, not the depositor).
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker observes an open channel. 2) Attacker calls addDeposit(channelId, amount) with their own tokens. 3) Channel deposit increases; attacker's tokens are now locked and will be refunded to the payer on finalize, not the attacker. 4) Attacker can also spam tiny deposits to bloat state and confuse off-chain accounting.
hypotheses.impact: Attacker's own funds are permanently lost (refunded to payer), and channel accounting/off-chain reconciliation is corrupted. No direct theft, but griefing and fund lock for the attacker.
hypotheses.recommendation: Require msg.sender == channel.payer in addDeposit(), or explicitly document and gate who may top up.

hypotheses.title: finalize() callable by anyone after grace period, forcing premature closure
hypotheses.description: finalize() has no access control beyond the grace-period check. Combined with the unrestricted initiateClose(), any external actor can force a channel to close after the grace period, refunding the payer and cutting off the payee. Even without initiateClose, once a legitimate close is initiated, any third party can finalize.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker calls initiateClose(channelId). 2) Waits GRACE_PERIOD. 3) Calls finalize(channelId). 4) Channel is marked finalized; payee can no longer settle vouchers; payer gets refund.
hypotheses.impact: Premature termination of streaming payment channels; payee loses future revenue; griefing vector.
hypotheses.recommendation: Restrict finalize() to channel.payer or channel.payee, or require both parties' consent.

hypotheses.title: close() allows voucher.cumulativeAmount > deposit causing zero payee payment
hypotheses.description: In close(), the payee transfer is guarded by `delta > 0 && delta <= channel.deposit`, but `delta = cumulativeAmount - settled`. If the signed voucher's cumulativeAmount exceeds channel.deposit (e.g., payer topped up incorrectly, or signer authorized more than deposit), the payee branch is skipped silently while `payerRefund = deposit - cumulativeAmount` underflows and also skips. The channel still marks finalized, and the payee receives only prior settled amounts while the payer's full remaining deposit remains stuck in the contract.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Payer (or authorizedSigner) signs a final voucher whose cumulativeAmount > deposit (allowed, since settle() would revert but close() only checks the transfer guard). 2) Caller invokes close() with that voucher and a valid payer signature. 3) Both transfer branches are skipped due to guards; channel.finalized = true. 4) Remaining tokens are permanently locked in the contract with no recovery function.
hypotheses.impact: Payee is underpaid relative to the owed cumulative amount, and the difference between deposit and settled is permanently frozen in the contract (loss of funds / insolvency of the channel accounting model).
hypotheses.recommendation: Revert if voucher.cumulativeAmount > channel.deposit, and compute payeeAmount = voucher.cumulativeAmount - channel.settled unconditionally to transfer correctly; do not rely on guard fallthroughs.

hypotheses.title: Cooperative close double-charges settled amount to payer refund
hypotheses.description: In `close()`, the payer refund is computed as `channel.deposit - voucher.cumulativeAmount`, but `channel.settled` may already be less than `voucher.cumulativeAmount` while part of the deposit was already paid out to the payee via prior `settle()` calls. The `delta` transferred to payee covers only the incremental amount, yet the refund subtracts the full cumulative amount from the deposit, which is correct for the total, but the check neglects the case where `channel.settled` was already partially paid. Actually the real bug is that `channel.settled` is never updated in `close()`, and if the same voucher (same nonce) is replayed after close on a *different* channel-id collision—no, the channel is finalized. The concrete issue: `delta = voucher.cumulativeAmount - channel.settled` can underflow if the provided voucher's cumulativeAmount is lower than already-settled amount, reverting the whole close and permanently bricking cooperative close for that channel because the check is missing.
hypotheses.attackPath: Payee (or channel partner) settles a high voucher normally; then when payer wants cooperative close with a lower cumulative value (e.g., off-chain revised accounting), `delta` underflows (0.8.20 reverts), so `close()` always reverts. Neither party can ever cooperatively close; payer is forced to wait out grace period. More critically, if the payee's high voucher was settled, and the payer signs a lower close voucher, the transaction reverts—griefing the cooperative path.
hypotheses.impact: Cooperative close path becomes unreachable once any settlement exceeds a proposed close voucher, forcing grace-period finalize and losing immediate settlement UX; also `settled` is not updated in `close()` leading to inconsistent state if partial settlement existed (payer refund uses `deposit - cumulativeAmount` which ignores previously transferred settled amounts, potentially over-refunding payer if `settled > 0`).
hypotheses.recommendation: Require `voucher.cumulativeAmount >= channel.settled`, update `channel.settled = voucher.cumulativeAmount` inside `close()`, and compute refund as `channel.deposit - voucher.cumulativeAmount` only after verifying no underflow.

hypotheses.title: close() CLOSE signature lacks nonce, expiry, and domain binding
hypotheses.description: The payer's CLOSE authorization is computed as `keccak256(abi.encodePacked("CLOSE", channelId, cumulativeAmount))` wrapped in an Ethereum Signed Message prefix. It contains no nonce, no expiry, and no chainId/contract address. A payer signature for one close can be reused for any future close with the same channelId and cumulativeAmount, and the same signature is valid across chains and across any contract that uses the same scheme.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Payer signs a CLOSE authorization for a cooperative close. 2) Payee does not use it immediately. 3) Later, payee (or any holder) replays the same signature to force a close on a re-opened channel with the same channelId (channelId is deterministic from payer/payee/token/timestamp/counter, so collisions are possible) or on a forked chain.
hypotheses.impact: Unauthorized channel closure and fund movement using a stale payer signature; cross-chain replay.
hypotheses.recommendation: Use EIP-712 with a dedicated CLOSE typehash including channelId, cumulativeAmount, nonce, expiry, and rely on the domain separator for chain/contract binding.

hypotheses.title: addDeposit() allows anyone to deposit, but refund goes to payer
hypotheses.description: `addDeposit()` calls `channel.token.safeTransferFrom(msg.sender, address(this), amount)` but does not verify `msg.sender == channel.payer`. Any external actor can add deposit to a channel, but on finalize/close the entire deposit (including the third-party contribution) is refunded to `channel.payer`. This allows a griefer to donate funds to a payer, or more subtly, a payer can use a third party to top up and then claim the refund.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker calls `addDeposit(channelId, amount)` on a victim's channel. 2) Attacker's tokens are transferred into the channel. 3) On finalize, the entire deposit (including attacker's contribution) is refunded to `channel.payer`. 4) Attacker loses funds; payer gains them.
hypotheses.impact: Third-party depositors lose funds to the payer; griefing vector where attacker can inflate a channel's deposit and then the payer claims the refund.
hypotheses.recommendation: Require `msg.sender == channel.payer` in `addDeposit()`, or track per-depositor balances.

hypotheses.title: close() allows underflow revert and inconsistent refund when cumulativeAmount > deposit
hypotheses.description: In close(), delta = voucher.cumulativeAmount - channel.settled is computed without checking cumulativeAmount >= channel.settled, and payerRefund = channel.deposit - voucher.cumulativeAmount is computed without checking voucher.cumulativeAmount <= channel.deposit. If the authorized signer signs a voucher with cumulativeAmount > deposit (or < settled), the subtraction underflows and reverts (Solidity 0.8 checked math), bricking the cooperative close path. More critically, the payee transfer is guarded by `delta <= channel.deposit` but the guard compares delta to deposit rather than to (deposit - settled), so a voucher with cumulativeAmount between settled and deposit can still pass while the refund branch silently skips (payerRefund > 0 && payerRefund <= channel.deposit), leaving funds stranded in the contract with channel.finalized = true.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) A malicious or buggy authorized signer (or a payer colluding) signs a voucher with cumulativeAmount > channel.deposit. 2) Anyone calls close(); the subtraction `channel.deposit - voucher.cumulativeAmount` underflows and reverts, permanently blocking cooperative close. 3) Alternatively, with cumulativeAmount slightly above deposit but delta <= deposit, the payee transfer succeeds while payerRefund underflows/skips, and channel.finalized is set true — remaining tokens are locked forever since finalize() reverts on finalized channels.
hypotheses.impact: Permanent lock of channel funds (frozen tokens) and/or DoS of the cooperative close path; accounting inconsistency between settled, deposit, and actual token balance.
hypotheses.recommendation: Add explicit checks: require(voucher.cumulativeAmount >= channel.settled) and require(voucher.cumulativeAmount <= channel.deposit) before computing delta/refund; use the same delta guard as settle().

hypotheses.title: close() does not update settledNonces, allowing replay via settle()
hypotheses.description: `close()` sets `channel.finalized = true` but never updates `settledNonces[channelId]`. Since `settle()` checks `channel.finalized` and reverts, replay via settle is blocked. However, the nonce is not recorded, so any off-chain accounting or future upgrade that relies on `settledNonces` will be inconsistent. More critically, if `close()` is called with a voucher whose nonce is lower than a previously settled nonce, the channel is finalized with a stale cumulativeAmount, and the payee loses the difference.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Payee settles voucher V1 (nonce=5, cumulativeAmount=100). 2) Payer signs close voucher V2 (nonce=3, cumulativeAmount=50) — perhaps a stale voucher. 3) Payee calls close(V2, ...) — no nonce check, so V2 is accepted. 4) Payee receives delta = 50 - 100 → underflow revert, or if settled=0, payee receives 50 instead of 100, and payer refunds 50. Payee loses 50.
hypotheses.impact: Payee can be forced to accept a lower cumulativeAmount via a stale close voucher, losing funds; or the close reverts due to underflow, bricking cooperative close.
hypotheses.recommendation: Add `if (voucher.nonce <= settledNonces[voucher.channelId]) revert NonceTooLow();` and update `settledNonces` in `close()`.

hypotheses.title: settle() allows payee to grief payer by settling after close initiated
hypotheses.description: `initiateClose()` sets `gracePeriodEnd` but does not block `settle()` from being called during the grace period. This is intended, but combined with `close()` (cooperative close) which sets `finalized = true` without checking `gracePeriodEnd`, a payee holding a valid voucher can settle during the grace period and then the payer's cooperative close signature (signed earlier for a lower cumulative amount) becomes unusable, or vice versa. More critically, `close()` does not verify `voucher.nonce > settledNonces[channelId]`, so a payee can replay an old voucher in `close()` after a newer voucher was already settled in `settle()`, causing `delta = voucher.cumulativeAmount - channel.settled` to underflow-revert or, if cumulativeAmount is higher, double-count.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Payer opens channel, payee settles voucher with cumulativeAmount=100, nonce=5. 2) Payee obtains a payer-signed CLOSE message for cumulativeAmount=100 (or any value). 3) Payee calls `close()` with the same voucher; `settledNonces` is not checked, `channel.settled` is still 100, so `delta = 100 - 100 = 0`, no double payment — but if payee uses a *different* voucher with cumulativeAmount=200 and a stale nonce, `delta = 200 - 100 = 100` is paid even though the nonce was already used, bypassing replay protection.
hypotheses.impact: Replay of vouchers via `close()` bypasses the nonce check enforced in `settle()`, allowing payee to extract funds using stale/replayed vouchers, draining the channel deposit beyond what the payer authorized.
hypotheses.recommendation: In `close()`, enforce `voucher.nonce > settledNonces[voucher.channelId]` and update `settledNonces` before transferring, mirroring `settle()`.

hypotheses.title: close() trusts payerSignature without binding to expiry or nonce, enabling replay
hypotheses.description: The `closeDigest` is computed as `keccak256("\x19Ethereum Signed Message:\n32", keccak256(("CLOSE", channelId, cumulativeAmount)))`. It does not bind the nonce or expiry, and it is separate from the EIP-712 domain (no chainId / contract address). This signature is replayable across chains (same contract address on Tempo mainnet/testnet) and reusable for any voucher at the same cumulativeAmount. A payee who once received a CLOSE signature for amount X can re-submit it with any voucher (signed by authorizedSigner) whose cumulativeAmount is X, at any point in the future, as long as nonce check is bypassed by missing settledNonces update — and indeed close() never updates settledNonces.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Payer truthfully signs CLOSE for amount X for a legitimate close. 2) Later the payer wants to close at Y ≠ X (or on a different chain). 3) Payee reuses the old CLOSE signature with a fresh voucher expiring now (expiry unchecked in close) and cumAmount X. 4) Because close() does not update settledNonces and does not check voucher.nonce against settledNonces beyond nothing — no check at all — the replay succeeds. Funds drained.
hypotheses.impact: Payer loses funds to a stale cooperative-close signature; cross-chain replay amplifies impact to all deployments with same bytecode.
hypotheses.recommendation: Use EIP-712 typed structured data including domain separator, nonce and expiry; store and check nonce in close().

hypotheses.title: close() payerSignature uses non-EIP-712 scheme, enabling cross-context replay
hypotheses.description: The payer's authorization in close() is verified against a personal_sign-style digest (keccak256("\x19Ethereum Signed Message:\n32", keccak256(abi.encodePacked("CLOSE", channelId, cumulativeAmount)))). This digest is not bound to the contract address or chainId, so a payer signature collected for one deployment/chain can be replayed on another deployment of the same contract with the same channelId and cumulativeAmount. It also lacks a nonce, so the same payerSignature can be reused across multiple close() attempts on the same channel (though finalized blocks repeats).
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Payer signs a CLOSE authorization for channelId C and amount A on chain X. 2) Attacker replays the same payerSignature on chain Y (or a redeployed contract) where a channel with the same channelId C exists. 3) close() accepts the signature and finalizes the channel without the payer's fresh consent on that chain.
hypotheses.impact: Cross-chain / cross-deployment replay of payer close authorizations; unauthorized channel finalization.
hypotheses.recommendation: Use EIP-712 with the contract's domain separator (address + chainId) for the payer close authorization, and include a nonce.

hypotheses.title: settle() allows delta beyond available deposit via unchecked subtraction path
hypotheses.description: settle() computes `delta = voucher.cumulativeAmount - channel.settled` and then checks `delta > channel.deposit - channel.settled`. Because channel.settled is set to cumulativeAmount after the check, and cumulativeAmount could be less than channel.settled (a replayed lower cumulative with higher nonce), the subtraction `voucher.cumulativeAmount - channel.settled` underflows and reverts — but more importantly the check itself is insufficient: the correct invariant is `voucher.cumulativeAmount <= channel.deposit`. The code only checks the delta against remaining balance and does not enforce monotonicity of cumulativeAmount, so a signed voucher with cumulativeAmount < settled and higher nonce reverts the settle, potentially DoS-ing payee settlements and blocking the channel's progress.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) authorizedSigner (compromised or mistaken) signs voucher where cumulativeAmount < channel.settled with a higher nonce. 2) Payee calls settle(); arithmetic underflow reverts the transaction. 3) Payee cannot settle, cannot progress the nonce, and any subsequent legit voucher with the same or lower nonce is blocked until a strictly increasing nonce with cumulativeAmount >= settled is provided.
hypotheses.impact: Denial of settlement / progress for the channel; used with the expiry and nonce mechanisms, can strand funds and permanently block payee from claiming owed amounts.
hypotheses.recommendation: Explicitly require `voucher.cumulativeAmount >= channel.settled` and `voucher.cumulativeAmount <= channel.deposit` before computing delta; reject non-monotonic cumulative amounts.

hypotheses.title: settle() allows cumulativeAmount to decrease, enabling negative delta underflow
hypotheses.description: `settle()` computes `delta = voucher.cumulativeAmount - channel.settled` without verifying `voucher.cumulativeAmount >= channel.settled`. The only nonce check is `voucher.nonce > settledNonces[channelId]`, which is independent of cumulativeAmount. A payee (or anyone holding a valid signed voucher with a higher nonce but lower cumulativeAmount) can submit it, causing the subtraction to underflow and revert — but more importantly, if the authorized signer signs a voucher with a lower cumulativeAmount and higher nonce (e.g., due to off-chain bug or malicious signer), the subtraction reverts, bricking settlement. Conversely, if cumulativeAmount < settled but the subtraction is unchecked in some path, it would credit the payee incorrectly.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Authorized signer signs voucher V1 with cumulativeAmount=100, nonce=1. 2) Payee settles V1, channel.settled=100, settledNonces=1. 3) Signer (or attacker who compromises signer) signs V2 with cumulativeAmount=50, nonce=2. 4) Payee calls settle(V2) — `delta = 50 - 100` underflows and reverts (Solidity 0.8 checked math). This is a DoS but not theft. However, if the signer is the payer's delegate and signs a lower cumulativeAmount with higher nonce, the payee cannot settle, and the channel is stuck until close/finalize.
hypotheses.impact: Settlement can be permanently bricked if a lower-cumulativeAmount voucher with higher nonce is signed; payee loses ability to claim funds until grace period finalize, and payer can grief by signing such vouchers.
hypotheses.recommendation: Add `if (voucher.cumulativeAmount < channel.settled) revert InvalidAmount();` before computing delta.

hypotheses.title: finalize() callable by anyone, allowing premature refund to payer
hypotheses.description: `finalize()` has no caller restriction. After the grace period ends, any address can call it, refunding the payer and marking the channel finalized. Combined with the unrestricted `initiateClose()`, an attacker can force-close a channel and then finalize it, preventing the payee from settling any voucher issued after the grace period started (since `settle()` reverts on `finalized`).
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker calls `initiateClose(channelId)`. 2) Attacker waits 1 hour. 3) Attacker calls `finalize(channelId)`, refunding payer and setting `finalized=true`. 4) Payee's pending vouchers can no longer be settled.
hypotheses.impact: Payee loses earned payments for services rendered during the grace period; payer gets refunded for services already consumed.
hypotheses.recommendation: Restrict `finalize()` to `channel.payer` or `channel.payee`, and/or extend grace period logic to allow payee settlement.

hypotheses.title: close() lacks expiry check enabling stale voucher replay within cooperative close
hypotheses.description: Unlike `settle()`, the `close()` function does not check `block.timestamp > voucher.expiry`. A payee and any address holding a payer's "CLOSE" signature (which only binds channelId and cumulativeAmount) can settle a voucher after its expiry as long as the payer's CLOSE signature matches the same cumulativeAmount. If a payer pre-signs CLOSE messages in advance (common in cooperative workflows), a stale authorization can be reused with any voucher signed by authorizedSigner that has the same cumulativeAmount — bypassing expiry guarantees.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Payer pre-signs CLOSE(channelId, X) off-chain. 2) Later payer intends to close at amount Y < X. 3) Payee obtains the old CLOSE signature and a voucher for X from authorizedSigner with an expired expiry. 4) Payee calls close() with these — passes because expiry is unchecked — drains deposit to payee at stale amount X.
hypotheses.impact: Payee can force settlement at a higher cumulative amount than the payer intended at close time; payer loses funds.
hypotheses.recommendation: Add `if (block.timestamp > voucher.expiry) revert VoucherExpired();` in close(), and include expiry in the signed CLOSE digest.

hypotheses.title: settle() does not verify caller is payee, allowing anyone to force settlement
hypotheses.description: settle() has no check that msg.sender is the channel's payee. Any external actor holding a valid signed voucher (e.g., obtained from the payee's HTTP 402 response, mempool, or a leaked signature) can call settle() and force the transfer of channel tokens to the payee. While funds go to the correct payee, this lets an untrusted third party advance channel state (settled, settledNonces) and consume the voucher's nonce, potentially interfering with the payee's intended settlement ordering or expiry handling.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker obtains a valid voucher+signature (e.g., intercepted from the 402 PaymentAuth flow or a public relay). 2) Attacker calls settle(voucher, signature) before the payee does. 3) State advances: settledNonces updated, channel.settled increased, tokens sent to payee. 4) Payee's later attempt with a different voucher may be blocked by nonce ordering or expiry.
hypotheses.impact: Unauthorized state mutation of channel accounting; potential denial of settlement for the legitimate payee if nonce ordering is disrupted.
hypotheses.recommendation: Require msg.sender == channel.payee in settle() (and in close()).

hypotheses.title: close() does not update channel.settled or settledNonces, breaking state consistency
hypotheses.description: close() sets channel.finalized = true and transfers funds, but never updates channel.settled or settledNonces[channelId]. This leaves the channel's stored accounting inconsistent with the actual settled amount. Any downstream logic or off-chain indexer reading getChannel()/settledNonces will see stale values (settled = 0, nonce = 0) even though the channel is finalized and funds have moved. If any future code path (or an upgrade) relies on these fields, it will compute wrong refunds/deltas.
hypotheses.attackPath: An untrusted actor cannot directly exploit this in the current code, but any integration (indexer, future upgrade, or a second contract reading channel state) will misreport settled amounts and nonces, leading to incorrect accounting. Combined with the missing finalized guard on getAvailableBalance, off-chain consumers may believe funds remain available.
hypotheses.impact: Wrong accounting / stale state exposed to integrators; potential for downstream contracts to miscompute balances.
hypotheses.recommendation: In close(), set channel.settled = voucher.cumulativeAmount and settledNonces[channelId] = voucher.nonce before finalizing.

hypotheses.title: settle() allows cumulativeAmount below channel.settled causing underflow revert / griefing
hypotheses.description: settle() computes delta = voucher.cumulativeAmount - channel.settled without checking voucher.cumulativeAmount >= channel.settled. If a signed voucher with a lower cumulativeAmount but higher nonce is submitted, the subtraction underflows and reverts (Solidity 0.8.x). While this reverts rather than corrupts state, it means a payee holding a valid higher-nonce but lower-cumulative voucher cannot settle, and the nonce check (voucher.nonce > settledNonces) passes before the underflow, so the revert is the only guard.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Payer signs a voucher with cumulativeAmount lower than already settled but higher nonce (e.g., due to off-chain bug or malicious payer). 2) Payee calls settle(); nonce check passes, then subtraction underflows and reverts. 3) Payee cannot settle; channel stuck until close/finalize.
hypotheses.impact: Denial of settlement for the payee; channel can only be resolved via close() or finalize().
hypotheses.recommendation: Add an explicit check `if (voucher.cumulativeAmount < channel.settled) revert InvalidAmount();` before computing delta.

hypotheses.title: First-depositor/donation attack via direct token transfer to contract
hypotheses.description: The contract tracks deposits in `channel.deposit` but holds tokens in a shared balance across all channels. Any external actor can transfer tokens directly to the contract address. Since finalize() refunds exactly `channel.deposit - channel.settled`, direct donations accumulate uncounted. Conversely, if any code path (like close() with underflow guards) leaves tokens stranded, they are permanently locked because there is no sweep. There is also no per-channel solvency accounting that reconciles actual token balance with the sum of deposits.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker directly transfers tokens to the contract (donation). 2) No channel balance is updated; the tokens are stuck forever as there is no rescue/sweep function. 3) Additionally, a malicious token with fee-on-transfer semantics would cause deposit in the struct to exceed actual received amount, so settle()/finalize() would revert on insufficient real balance and lock the channel.
hypotheses.impact: Donated or fee-on-transfer-reduced tokens become permanently locked; the contract's real token balance drifts below the sum of channel deposits, enabling insolvency of later settlements.
hypotheses.recommendation: Either add a token rescue function callable for unrelated tokens, or (preferred) support only non-fee-on-transfer tokens and require the actual received amount to be measured via balance delta before crediting channel.deposit.

hypotheses.title: settle() retains over-signed voucher allowing payee underpayment path in close()
hypotheses.description: close() does not update settledNonces nor channel.settled (it only sets finalized), and it uses `voucher.cumulativeAmount` for both payee payment and payer refund computation without reconciling against channel.settled or settledNonces. If the same voucher was already partially settled via settle(), then close() will compute `delta = cumulativeAmount - settled` correctly for payee but `payerRefund = deposit - cumulativeAmount` uses the full cumulative, not remaining after prior settlements, causing double counting: the payee receives the new delta while the payer refund ignores prior settlements — correct in this case, but close() also does not advance settledNonces, so a replay pattern across multiple channels with shared nonces is not blocked.
hypotheses.attackPath: See above narration.
hypotheses.impact: Voucher replay across channels (since nonce is global per channelId, not per payer), and potential accounting drift if settle() was called before close() with a higher nonce and lower cumulative, causing inconsistency.
hypotheses.recommendation: Require `voucher.nonce > settledNonces[channelId]` in close() and store it, plus require cumulativeAmount >= channel.settled.

hypotheses.title: close() uses cumulativeAmount directly without clamping, delta only guarded by `<= deposit`
hypotheses.description: In `close()`, `delta = voucher.cumulativeAmount - channel.settled` — if `voucher.cumulativeAmount < channel.settled`, this underflows and reverts (Solidity 0.8). But if `voucher.cumulativeAmount > channel.deposit`, the `delta <= deposit` check uses delta vs deposit, not against `deposit - settled`, allowing delta up to `channel.deposit`. That means a malicious payee can pass delta == deposit even when settled > 0, transferring a full deposit-worth of tokens to payee on top of already-settled amounts — overpaying payee by `settled` and leaving payerRefund underflow.
hypotheses.attackPath: Suppose deposit=100, settled=80. Payee passes cumulativeAmount=100 (<=deposit). delta=20. Check `20 <= 100` passes. Payee gets 20 (correct). But suppose payee passes cumulativeAmount=180 — wait, delta=100 <= 100 passes, but that's an over-settle; actually delta 100 vs deposit 100 passes, then payerRefund = 100-180 underflows → reverts. So underflow protects partially. However, with settled>0 and cumulativeAmount=deposit, no oracle prevents over-payment beyond voucher signer's authorization — signer is trusted so this is bounded. Still, the check `delta <= deposit` is weaker than `delta <= deposit - settled`.
hypotheses.impact: Inconsistent accounting compared to settle(); allows corrupt state math on attacker-controlled amounts with an unsuspecting signer.
hypotheses.recommendation: Change to `uint256 available = channel.deposit - channel.settled; require(delta <= available);`.
